MR. BALDWIN-OBJECTION TO CERTAIN INSTRUCTIONS TO COMMITTEE CHAIRMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which affects the rights and privileges of every member of this House in a very serious way.
I have given Your Honour the notice as is required, of course, by the Standing Order.
I have here What purports to be a copy of a letter written by the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader, presumably, with the rigid discipline that applies in this case, including the consent, knowledge, and approval of the government House leader. It is dated March 26, 1974. There are three very brief paragraphs which I feel I must read in order to lay the foundation for the development of this very serious breach of privilege by the hon. member.
The letter is addressed to committee chairmen and the subject is committee reports and estimates. We have heard of papal bulls; this is parliamentary bull being handed down by the hon. member.
The second paragraph states:
For your information and guidance-
This is the hon. member giving guidance to the committee chairmen who presumably have or should have the qualities of the Chair in regard to independence and objectivity in their approach to the problems that are placed before them. To begin again, the second paragraph of this amazing letter states:
For your information and guidance please note that reports from standing committees dealing with estimates should-
The letter does not say "ought"; it says "should". It continues:
-consist of approval, reduction, or elimination of estimates only.
The word "only" is in capital letters and underlined.

I believe that is indicated in citation 158, page 134, paragraph 3, which reads as follows:
An unsigned letter should not be read in the House. On the 16th May 1928, a member stated during debate that a letter which he had been quoting was not signed. speechtext: Has the Minister of Finance, or the Inspector-General of Banks acting for the minister, since March 14, 1973, had any further discussions with the chartered banks concerning the need for the pensions paid to their retired employees to be escalated annually by an amount at least equal to the rise in the cost of living and, if so, can the minister now say whether the chartered banks are implementing this practice with respect to their retired employees?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: PENSIONS FOR RETIRED CHARTERED BANK EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
As
indicated in the reply on March 14, 1973, the hon. member's starred questions numbered 811 and 1082 were drawn to the attention of the president of each of the chartered banks. subsubtopic: INCOME TAX-DEDUCTION OF MORTGAGE DEPRECIATION
speechtext: I assume that "depreciation" should be construed as "interest", and hence the proposal is for the deduction of mortgage interest in arriving at taxable income. speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the House have before them a legislation to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. These three acts are well known to the House. They allow the Minister of Finance to guarantee term loans granted by chartered banks and other designated financial institutions, loans granted to farmers, small businessmen and fishermen in order to finance a variety of improvements requiring capital expenditures for their business operations.
Under the existing provisions of each act these programs would expire on June 30, 1974, and one of the purposes of Bill C-14 is to provide for the continuation of these programs for a three-year period beyond that date. Before discussing the detailed provisions of this bill I would like to comment on each individual program.
The Farm Improvement Loans Act was implemented in 1944, initially for a three-year period. It has been amended on numerous occasions to add new lending periods and to enlarge the benefits available to farmers qualifying under the act. Presently, farmers may borrow up to $15,000 to help finance the acquisition of farm implements, buildings, equipment or livestock, and to repair or improve assets which are used in their farming enterprises. In addition, farmers may borrow up to $15,000 for the purchase of small parcels of land to round out an existing farm unit. The total amount which may be outstanding to any farmer at any time is $25,000 for all loan purposes.
The maximum period over which repayment may be spread varies with the purpose for which the loan was obtained and ranges from three years, in the case of trucks, to 15 years in the case of land purchase loans. The Farm Improvement Loans Act has played a crucial role in the financing of Canadian agriculture, as is evidenced by the fact that almost $3 billion have been loaned during almost 30 years of operations under the act. Lending activity in the 12 months to December 31, 1973, amounted to some $230 million, which is the largest volume of loans ever made in one year under this plan. Claims paid under this program have been remarkably low and amount to about one-fifth of one per cent of the face value of loans made.
The Fisheries Improvement Loans Act came into effect in 1955, also for an initial three-year period, and has subsequently been extended and amended from time to time. Under the current provisions of the act, fishermen

may borrow up to $25,000 to help finance the purchase, construction or repair of fishing vessels and equipment. The development of shore installations and equipment, which are a necessary part of a fishing enterprise, is also an eligible loan purpose. Borrowers may take up to ten years to repay most loans, although in the case of loans for certain purposes the maximum repayment period is shorter, more closely approximating the useful life of the asset being acquired. Lending under this program remained at relatively low levels for several years. More recently, however, there has been a marked increase in lending activity. In the year ending March 31, 1973, fisheries improvement loans reached a peak and amounted to $7 million. Claims have also been very low under this program, totally less than one-fifth of one per cent. Returns in the current loan year to date indicate that lending under this program is continuing at this high level.
The Small Businesses Loans Act came into effect in early 1961 for a three-year period and, like the other acts, has been extended and amended from time to time since. The legislation provides for loans of up to $25,000 to assist operators of small businesses in financing improvements in their business enterprises. In order to qualify, an enterprise must have gross annual revenue of less than $500,000 and must be engaged in one of the following forms of business activity-manufacturing, retail or wholesale trade, provision of services, construction, transportation or communications. Loans may be used to assist in acquiring fixed or moveable equipment or for the purchase, construction or renovation of business premises. Since inception, including the last full year of operation, $290 million have been made available to small businesses under the provisions of this legislation. Lending reached a peak of $30 million in the year ended December 31, 1973. Losses under this legislation have again been very small, being of the order of one half of one per cent. Indications are that lending under this program is also continuing at a high level.
A number of general provisions apply in connection with loans made under each of the programs. Borrowers are required to pledge security for loans, generally by way of a charge on the assets acquired with the loan and by giving a promissory note. In certain circumstances additional security may be required by the lender. Potential borrowers must also be prepared to make a minimum investment of their own in the project for which they seek a loan.
There is also a maximum rate of interest which lenders may charge on loans. Maximum interest rates are determined semi-annually on April 1 and October 1 of each year. The rates are based on the average yields of selected government of Canada bonds over a six-month period, to which is added a margin of 1 per cent. The maximum rate which can be charged during the period which commenced on April 1, 1974, is 8 per cent for loans made under the Small Businesses Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act for all loan purposes except the purchase of additional land. The maximum rate for land purchase loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, currently 8.25 per cent, is determined by a slightly different formula which is designed to reflect the fact that farmers may take up to 15 years to repay these loans.
April 10, 1974

As I indicated earlier, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-14 provides for a continuation of these lending programs for the three-year period July 1, 1974, to June 30, 1977. The bill also sets out amendments to the various acts, resulting from a major review of the effectiveness of the programs and from discussions and suggestions received from various interested groups. I shall deal with the amendments proposed for each act separately.
With respect to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the bill proposes the following changes in addition to the extension of the legislation for three years:
1.	To raise the maximum amount which may be advanced during the three-year period ending June 30, 1977, by lenders under guarantee of the minister to $1,100 million for loans made by chartered banks and $300 million for loans made by other lenders.
2.	To raise the maximum amount which a borrower may have outstanding to $50,000. The sub-limits are to be dropped.
3.	To extend the eligible purposes to include major repairs and overhaul of equipment and implements.
4.	To allow joint borrowers to have only their share of such borrowing count against their entitlement under the plan.
5.	To provide that the Alberta Treasury branches be permitted to make loans under the plan.
With respect to the Small Businesses Loans Act, the bill proposes the following changes:
1.	To raise the maximum amount which may be advanced during the three-year period ending June 30, 1977, by lenders under guarantee of the minister to $250 million for loans made by chartered banks and $100 million for loans made by other lenders.
2.	To raise the maximum amount which a borrower may have outstanding to $50,000.
3.	To change the definition of eligible businesses to make new businesses eligible to borrow.
4.	To change the definition of small business to mean one where estimated gross annual revenue for a fiscal year does not exceed $1 million.
5.	To extend the eligible purposes to allow for the purchase of land necessary for the operation of the eligible business.
6.	To provide that the Alberta Treasury branches be permitted to make loans under the plan.
With respect to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, the bill proposes the following changes:
1.	To raise the maximum amount which may be advanced by lenders under guarantee of the minister to $60 million for loans made by chartered banks and $10 million for loans made by other lenders.
2.	To raise the maximum amount which a borrower may have outstanding to $50,000.
The bill also provides for an increase of $5 million in the amount which may be loaned under the guarantee in respect of the current lending period ending on June 30, 1974. Lending in recent months by the chartered banks has shown a substantial rise, and unless the loan pool is
Loans Acts Amendments
enlarged banks will cease to make these loans when the current ceiling of $20 million is reached, probably in April or May, 1974.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize that these measures have been instrumental in the provision of intermediate and longer term funds for farmers, fishermen and small businessmen. The government believes that these programs should be extended for a further three-year period and that the amendments proposed for the various acts will enhance the value of these programs to the various groups they benefit.

I shall leave my parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Comtois), in charge of this debate.
As for me, I must appear before the Standing Committee of Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, pursuant to an order issued by that committee.
So, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I leave my parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Terrebonne, in charge of the debate.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister has indicated, this bill is actually a compendium of amendments to three acts, all of a similar type, dealing with loans that can be made available under government guarantee from chartered banks. We see the government has realized that inflation has caused an impact and that the three acts are meaningless without these amendments. It is not my intention to make any lengthy remarks on the individual parts of the act, but several of my colleagues will speak on specialities with regard to farm improvement loans, small businesses loans and fisheries improvement loans.
I am glad that my suggestion that we deal with this bill in committee of the whole was followed. One has to be realistic about the passage of legislation in this House. If hon. members want the fishermen or the small businessmen to benefit from these amendments, then the legislation must be put in the starting position and processed through to royal assent in the minimum of time. When one speaks of referring any item of business to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs it must be remembered that this government has not established its priorities. Including this item and one that was referred to the committee last week, that committee has for consideration seven major items in addition to the estimates.
We know that the discussions and hearings on the competition act will go on into June, so this bill would not be reported from committee until after that. I felt that was totally wrong. In light of the breakdown of negotiations for adjournment, the best use that could be made of today, and likely of tomorrow, would be to get this bill through all stages in the House. We could make shorter speeches to achieve this end.

April 10, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
I want to say something now about the increase in the ceilings of farm loans, small businesses loans and fisheries improvement loans to $50,000. I wish the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) were here. The other day he was guilty of the grossest inexactitude. I do not think it was deliberate, because I do not think he understands the Veterans Land Act. When my colleagues, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and others, asked for an increase in the ceilings under that act, he thought this was going to cost more money. He found it ridiculous for the opposition to advocate, on the one hand, the curtailing of government expenditure, and on the other to ask for greater government expenditure of this type.
That was utter tripe from the Prime Minister, because those loans are repayable; they are not an expense of government. If one followed the logic of the Prime Minister, one would say this is an increase in expenditure by the government. There is not any expenditure here by government, Mr. Speaker: the loans are made by the chartered banks or those that have status to make loans under the acts.
The ceilings of these loans are increased. It is true that there is a contingent liability under the guarantee, but when we are limited to one-tenth of the loans that may occur, the chances of a loan by a chartered bank or its equivalent are miniscule. The suggestion made by the Prime Minister the other day in trying to score a cheap political advantage did not have any substance whatsoever. I am sure if he were here this afternoon he would be trying to use the same sort of fallacious argument.
The small business enterprise is now deemed to be worth $1 million. This means we will have to review some of the other legislation such as the Canada Corporations Act. When we changed the law on Canadian corporations three years ago, they said if the sales volume is $3 million it is big business. Now we are getting into a small business with a ceiling on turnover of $1 million. These are some of the effects of inflation. Only when we see these practical examples of the day to day changes that have to be made in the law do we realize the type of cancer there is in this country at the present time against which this government is not taking action.
As the minister indicated this afternoon, the government tries to make changes by getting more income to certain people. What does that argument mean? If you are bleeding from a hole in the aorta, which is about as serious a condition as inflation in Canada today, when the minister says he will redistribute income that is equivalent to putting a band-aid on the exterior instead of performing the necessary surgery and maybe imposing restrictions to stop the bleeding. The government puts little band-aids on the outside, and we see the blood oozing all around, just as we see in the inflation all around the government programs.
Another argument with which the minister had difficulty was this. He talked about food prices and said we cannot really control them because so much of the food in Canada comes from outside the country, and therefore controls on food prices in this country would have little effect. But the third element of the problem is that we

must grow more of our own food in Canada although this will have little effect on inflation.
My colleagues will deal with the difficulties encountered in bank interest rates which today are over 9 per cent because of the mortgage rate. The fixed rates applicable to these programs under the guarantee make it impossible for the banks to make loans in the desired volume. The chartered banks are the only ones who deal with liquidity today, because the other institutions like the treasury branches, and so forth, must operate differently. They do not have the same formula for liquidity and so are restricted. The banks can operate with greater flexibility, but their liquidity was down to one-fifth of one per cent recently.
It is no wonder that money is tight with the banks in these circumstances and that they are only going to make loans which are most advantageous to them. They were never intended to be philanthropic institutions and that is not expected of them. Under these programs, however, there is a real problem and I believe my colleagues will point them out. We have to be realistic about this, so I hope we will have the appropriate number of speeches on second reading and then move to committee of the whole so the bill can be expedited and whatever limited benefits flow from these changes will be available to the appropriate classes in the Canadian economy.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe many small businessmen, farmers and fishermen will welcome this legislation.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: If they can get loans.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
As my colleague to my right says, if they can get loans. I suppose people who have taken out loans will take them out again, to meet present commitments, without thinking too much of the consequences in the future. The legislation reflects the changing conditions of farming and business. When the loan ceiling was $7,000 we thought we were doing well by increasing the ceiling to $15,000. This amendment would increase it to $50,000. It is true that farms, businesses and fisheries have become more mechanized and need more capital for electric power, internal combustion engines and other necessary equipment. Much of this increase is to offset the declining purchasing power of the dollar, of the money that is needed for capital or for repairing existing machinery.
Farm improvement loans are to be made for machinery repairs. It seems that the farmer cannot generate enough earning power to provide for the repair and maintenance of his machines; he must borrow money to keep his machines running. I am concerned that those responsible for planning the fiscal, financial and industrial policies of this country think that farm earnings will not provide for the repair and maintenance of machinery and that we must provide for guaranteed bank loans to cover these repairs. Or, to turn the argument around, do the financial institutions with whom the farmer must deal, the banks, credit unions and caisses populaires in rural communities not want to lend money for maintaining machines on the farm? Do they want to get out from under that risk and have the government of Canada assume the major
April 10, 1974

burden? Is that why we are being asked to approve loans, guaranteed by the citizens of Canada, which are to be used for maintaining farm machinery?
The chartered banks are in the business of lending money. Since we do not allow foreign banks to do much business in this country, I think it is the responsibility of our chartered banks, given these conditions, to lend money to farmers, small businessmen and fishermen for the ordinary operation of the farm, business or fishery. I am surprised that we need to guarantee bank loans to enable farmers to continue in the ordinary business of farming.
I do not oppose the bill. Probably it will provide an added service to the farmer. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary can say, since the minister is not present, whether this provision was brought forward at the request of the banks, at the request of farm organizations, or whether it originated with the government. Quite apart from the increased ceiling, it is a new departure. In the field of farm credit we badly need new policies and new directions on the part of government. We need new approaches in the field of loans to farmers. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has said we need changes. The deputy minister of agriculture for Saskatchewan, Mr. McArthur, has suggested the need for changes in that direction. In addition, the deputy minister of agriculture for Saskatchewan, the CFA and others have said it would be better if farm credit programs came under the control and direction of the provinces rather than under the control and direction of the federal government.
The other day we asked the officials of the Farm Credit Corporation what would be the effect of such policy on farm development policies and land transfer policies. We wanted to know what would happen in individual provinces with regard to the transfer of land and farms. In other words, we wanted to know what would be the effect on people operating farms. We were not given detailed information. It was not presented to the committee in a way which enabled us to make an assessment. We were given general information. When we or Crown agencies follow land policies which affect the social structure within a province and will eventually affect the farm structure within the province, the province should have the right to make major decisions involving that kind of policy. In this connection I quote the following:
Mr. Hamilton suggested that under such a system, Ottawa would provide the bulk of the funds to the provincial agency and participate in the development of national policy guidelines.
"With the credit actually being provided and administered at the provincial level, the lending function could be integrated into the provincial agricultural development program, within the national guidelines, including its agricultural extension services."
Such a system would not necessarily need to have its credit offices, he said. "If traditional lending services wished to participate in the system, the federal-provincial program could work with them by providing guarantees and developing expertise and counselling services."
Mr. Hamilton said such a system is needed because, even with improvements, the chartered banking system will not meet all the requirements as farmers see them.
That is what a person in one of the farm organizations is saying about our present credit system. He goes on at some length to deal with this problem. It is significant that the Federation of Agriculture as well as a deputy minister of
Loans Acts Amendments
one province made this point and made it very explicitly. I could also quote the deputy minister but I do not think that is necessary at the moment. I hope the government will take these points of view into account. They received recently a brief from the Federation of Agriculture. They have that in their hands. I do not know the response of the government to the representations made to them by the Federation of Agriculture with regard to several of these points.
The government failed to make changes in the bill which would make credit available to groups of farmers in adequate amounts. Maybe that is because the bill had already been drafted; I do not know. As I said, I did not see any signs in the Standing Committee on Agriculture of the government's advancing new approaches that are needed. They act as though not too much has changed and just go on doing business in their standard way.
What is going to be the method of setting the interest rates? What will control the interest rates? This question was raised by the previous speaker. Are we simply going to let the interest rate go up as it increases in the system or as the banks choose to increase it, or are we going to have some definite control? What is going to be the policy? Will it be an election boondoggle, or a policy, that we will have? A prize boondoggle which backfired occurred on September 28, 1972. On that date the then minister of agriculture, standing for election, sought to save himself by freezing the interest rate on farm improvement loans. The order in council reads:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, pursuant to section 6 of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, is pleased hereby to amend the Farm Improvement Loans regulations made by Order in Council P C. 1969592 of 25th March, 1969, as amended, in accordance with the schedule hereto.
The schedule reads:
1. Section 7 of the Farm Improvement Loans regulations is amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
"(6) Notwithstanding any other provision of this section, the base
rate for the interest period commencing on the 1st day of October,
1972, and ending on the 31st day of March, 1973, is,
(a)	in respect of a loan described in paragraph (2) (a), six per cent per annum; and
(b)	in respect of a loan described in paragraph (2)(b), five per cent per annum."
That was one of the most blatant manipulations of an interest rate under a federal act that had been pulled off for some time. One lesson the government might very well learn from it is that it did not work. The then minister of agriculture did not make it back here. It provided a very bad example for successive governments. It had the effect of temporarily drying up supplies of money under the Farm Improvement Loans Act for some months because of the unwillingness of the banks to lend money at that interest rate. I hope we will get some information on what is to be the interest policy under the regulations of this act. I hope the parliamentary secretary will give us more information this afternoon.
Another concern we should have about this kind of legislation is the ability of the farmer, businessman or fisherman to repay. Increased costs on the farm front will cut very deeply into the price structure with which the farmer is now living. It was interesting to hear the Prime

April 10, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
Minister (Mr. Trudeau) say this afternoon that one of the big factors affecting the cost of food is the international price structure around the world. He said, by inference, this is affecting the Canadian price structure.
I do not know at exactly what price the Canadian Wheat Board is selling wheat, but we can look at the Chicago market. Wheat has declined to almost $2. Corn has declined. Rapeseed and flaxseed have declined substantially. The prices of live beef and live pork have declined substantially. All this has been within the past few months.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: What about grain prices?

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: The hon. member asks about grain prices. Wheat prices have declined. You just do not have a system to get it to you.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: What are you quoting?

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
I am quoting international prices, because that is what the Prime Minister and other ministers were speaking about. Beef and pork, red meat, on the domestic market have declined in price. This is having an effect on the consumer. My point is that we are talking about a loan program for farmers who are dealing and living with an international market for their products. The market for their products fluctuates and there is very little market guarantee. The present market guarantee for hogs is so far below any market price that is significant that it just does not count. The same is true with the fisheries. Whether or not there is any real intention on the part of the government to change this situation, I do not know.
The Minister of Agriculture was asked about increased costs this afternoon and he blamed them on international factors. The bulk of our fertilizer, with the exception of imported phosphate rock from the United States, is manufactured in Canada. One of the sharpest rises in price of any commodity that the farmer uses is in the cost of twine. Sisal is imported. We also manufacture synthetic twine. In the area where I farm, most of the hay is tied with synthetic twine. I do not know why the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) permits such an outrageous price for synthetic twine. This is manufactured from by-products of refined petroleum.
Hon. members opposite get very excited about energy prices and want to keep the cost of petroleum, of the raw material, at what they say is a Canada-wide level. I refer to heating oil, gasoline, and so on. But why do not the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Consumer Affairs concern themselves about added costs that will accrue to the farmers for synthetic baling twine? I have had many telephone calls and letters about this.
Polyethylene baling twine is manufactured from a by-product of petroleum. We do not have to be totally dependent on offshore supplies of oil to get supplies of baling twine, though we are partially dependent. We do not have to let the oil companies overcharge the farmer and keep baling twine in short supply. This is what is happening, yet hon. members opposite show no concern. There is no use my quoting the price of baling twine

today. I talked to some people in Ontario the other day who were very closely connected with the business, and they told me the farmers will have to pay whatever somebody asks them to pay wherever they can find baling twine. I have been told by farming groups contracting in the Peace River country that they can no longer place any firm contracts.
We are only a few months away from the time when our farmers are going to tie up a lot of hay in this country, tons of it. Therefore, I would have thought that the minister would show some concern for this particular problem. If it is fair to hold down the price of gasoline to a certain level for people driving cars in Ottawa and Toronto, it should be equally fair to hold down the price of synthetic baler twine for a farmer baling hay in Saskatchewan. Both these groups are consumers.
As far as this lending program is concerned, if we are going to allow the price of baling twine, fertilizer, farm machinery products, anti-freeze and repairs to rise at the same rate as last year, then neither the government nor the banks will be able to loan the farmers enough money to keep them in operation. The industries that supply the farmer are getting all set to take him to the cleaners.
In my area, Mr. Speaker, one does not have to worry about lending the farmer a lot of money to buy tractors, because the farm machinery companies do not have any tractors for sale. I do not know what is happening in this regard, but it should be the business of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Minister of Agriculture to find out. If we have run out of steel supplies to make tractors and machinery parts, that is one thing. But I suspect that the farm machinery companies are doing to the farmers what the oil companies did to the economies of the United States and Canada. They were running consumers deliberately short of petroleum from the refineries and then jacking up the price, and I think the supply of farm machinery is being quite deliberately run down so that the price can be jacked up. The same thing is happening with the supply of other essentials to which I have referred today, such as baler twine, chemicals to control weeds and insects, fertilizer and farm machinery parts. If you go right through the book you get essentially the same pattern.
So far as transportation is concerned, we have one of the most inefficient transportation systems, in terms of annual operation, that we have ever had. Here again, this will cost us a great deal of money. We do not know when the situation will be corrected and we will be given the kind of service we need. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board talks of farmers hauling their grain "X" number of miles past their own delivery points to the railroad so they can get their grain off their farms this year. This is added cost both in money and in time.
Like the farmers, Mr. Speaker, the businessmen of Saskatchewan are also trying to survive. One of them asked me whether I would check why he had not received a reduction in price, as an independent handler, as a result of a tax cut at the wholesale level. The reduction in price had not been passed on to this small businessman. I told him that I would investigate it, but after a while he told me not to do so because they might cut him off entirely
April 10, 1974

and he said he would rather pay the extra money. This is the sort of thing that is happening.
It is significant that we are financing three groups of people-the farmers, who are small businessmen, the small businessmen themselves, and the fishermen who, again, are small businessmen. Why does the government finance these three groups within this sector of the economy? My answer to that question is, because the multinational corporations are able to pass on unnecessary charges and costs to this sector of the economy. That is the reason.
John Kenneth Galbraith, in his book, said they have a planned economy in the United States-and that goes for Canada as well-but that the economy is planned by multinational corporations who decide how it will run and how it will work. Then he said those same corporations prey on the unorganized and the unprotected sector which is made up of the very people to whom we are guaranteeing loans. This is the unprotected and vulnerable sector of the Canadian economy. One of the problems with this government is that it is prepared to guarantee loans so the banks can give them money, and that is fine because the banks will lend the money. But the government is not prepared to take tough, hard, concrete action to protect these people to whom we are giving ever increasing amounts of money. The government is not prepared to guarantee them the kind of protection they ought to have.
The government is prepared to sit quietly while these people are overcharged for baler twine and for fertilizer, for example. The government sits quietly while the packing companies and the retail chains overcharge for beef. This is where the government ought to be getting tough. Unless the government takes steps to see that this sector of the economy is protected and can survive and function, we will be back here next year, or two or three years from now, being asked for even bigger lending limits or, perhaps even worse, the banks will be here asking us to make good on some of the guarantees we will make under this legislation. There is a point at which this well will run dry; let us make no mistake about that.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since there seems to be co-operation in the House for the adoption of this bill and also from the official opposition, as shown by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), I would not like to enter this debate and prolong the adoption procedures of this very important bill.
I would only like to make a few comments. First I would like to commend the government and especially the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) for having submitted this very adequate measure.
In view of the government's intention to increase production to solve the problem we are now facing, in Canada as well as in other countries, the presentation of such a bill was in my opinion very important.
The member for Edmonton West has suggested to accelerate the adoption procedures of this bill by studying it after the debate of the second reading, in the Committee
Loans Acts Amendments
of the Whole, instead of referring it to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. He has given a few reasons by saying that many measures were referred to this committee and that we would have to wait until June or July to see it adopted.
But I think that in the mind of the hon. member for Edmonton West who has a lot of experience in Parliament there is that concern, or rather that desire, that desperate eagerness of the official opposition to have an election. He is afraid to go before the people, the voters in Edmonton West, without this very progressive bill to help farmers, small businessmen and fishermen. I realize that there are not many fishermen in Edmonton but there are elsewhere in Canada, and I imagine that the Tories if they want to make some progress will try to get the fishermen's votes.
Mr. Speaker, that is indeed what I see in the remarks by the hon. member for Edmonton West. Of course, this government is not like-and thank God for that-the party of the official opposition. If I remember well, the so-called ARDA act was passed in 1962, but no amount was set aside to help farmers. It is the party I have the honour to represent in this House, Mr. Speaker, and that is a well known fact, which insisted on the ARDA plan and ensured the major developments we now have in my area as in all eastern and western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I will now get back to the bill. I am satisfied, and I say so on behalf of farmers, small businessmen and fishermen, with that increase from $25,000 to $50,000 in the amount that can be guaranteed by the government and loaned by banks. I want to point out to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Comtois) and this government that farmers in my area are very disappointed at the way they are treated with respect to farm loans, specially in the Gaspe area.
When a farmer in my area applies for a farm loan he is put through piles of red tape and ends up being offered a clearly inadequate and ridiculously low amount.
For instance, when it comes to evaluating a farming business, some inspectors who come from God knows where, maybe the Montreal area, evaluate a business in the Gaspe Peninsula on the same basis as a farming business in the prosperous Montreal area. I believe that this is unjust for our farmers.
People often dare say that there are no farmers in the Gaspe Peninsula: there are, and if the Farm Loans Act were more adequate and if the people who administer it and the inspectors responsible for reporting on the farming business of the applicants were more just, there would perhaps be a greater number of prosperous farmers in our area, and we do have a few. If this were the case, fewer farmers would be refused a farm loan by the Farm Credit Corporation on the report of the more or less qualified inspectors who appreciate or evaluate the stock, the value of the property, of the land or of the buildings. Instead of going into a production which would allow them to live comfortably and provide for their families, these farmers must abandon their land and, since they do not have the necessary training to go into other fields, they swell the ranks of people on welfare.
I wanted to emphasize this fact and I should like to urge the hon. Minister of Finance, through his parliamentary

April 10, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
secretary, to consider my criticisms, because it is not the first year that I have heard farmers complain: I am by profession a notary. I have to review and complete files for farmers concerning farm loans, and during my career as a notary, which extends over more than 20 years, I have seen that in the Gaspe Peninsula, at least at the time when I practised my profession actively, the farmers of my area received no more than five loans from the Farm Credit Corporation. Why? Because its rules are too strict, and no consideration is given to the region in evaluating the property and assets of the farmers. In my opinion, our farmers, whether they be from the Gaspe Peninsula, from the Montreal area, from the west or from the east, have as much right to live as those who are advantaged by market and climate conditions.
I therefore trust that those remarks will not fall on deaf ears and that, in the future, our farmers will get more attention on the part of the inspectors who, in their reports, decide whether or not they will be entitled to a farm loan.
Contrary to farm loans, loans to small businesses have been of immeasurable help and have enabled several businessmen in my area to survive and even expand their businesses. That increase from $25,000 to $50,000 will certainly help, in view of the considerable increase in construction and equipment, and to a greater extent, both businessmen and merchants. The same goes for fishermen who, for the second time in less than a week, are being helped by the government of Canada; last week, with regard to subsidies for their fishing boats, the government changed the act and increased its help.
I therefore want to thank the minister and the government for having introduced those measures, those amendments to the law which will, I trust, give the help their beneficiaries are entitled to expect.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill I commend the previous speaker for bringing forward some very good points. However, he did refer to the statement of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) that we could perhaps get on with the business of an election. I think the farmers of western Canada and Canada generally would forgive us if we were out of this House for a few months, then came back and proceeded in a new direction. All we have been hearing from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is talk. It was mentioned in the Speech from the Throne that there would be a number of things done in respect of agriculture. We have not yet seen introduced any of the bills in this regard.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: There is one in the Senate.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
We have not seen the legislation which was promised for the benefit of Canada. It is time these bills were brought forward so that we could see if there really is something in store for western Canada.
Bill C-14 is not new legislation. It has to do with legislation that has been in place for some time. This legislation is very important to farmers, small businessmen and fish-

ermen of Canada. A number of the provisions of this legislation deal with housekeeping items such as increasing the period from 1974 until 1977. I am glad the government finally has come around to doing what the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) fought for the last time such a bill was before the House; that is, that the Treasury branches of Alberta be able to provide loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Small Businesses Loans Act.
This bank has been in place for a number of years and is in competition with the other banks and credit unions in Alberta. I think it is only fair that the farmers of Alberta should be able to go to the bank with which they deal in many cases in order to obtain a farm improvement loan. The main purposes originally for this legislation were the purchase of agricultural implements, new and used, the construction, repair or alteration of farm buildings, the purchase of livestock, the purchase of additional farmland, and general works for the improvement or development of a farm, including clearing and breaking of land, irrigation systems, farm electric systems, fencing and draining works.
When looking at these original purposes, I suggest the reason for the increase from $25,000 to $50,000 is abundantly clear. The price has not only doubled, but it has multiplied drastically in respect of most of these purposes. The price the farmers have to pay has in most cases increased several times. We might consider agricultural implements, for example. Most farmers have found that in the last five or ten years the price of tractors has doubled. In some cases the price has tripled. We find that the price many farmers in western Canada must pay for a tractor is $12,000.
Because of the inability to obtain labour, most farmers must face increased capitalization costs in order to purchase machinery. They can no longer obtain the necessary labour to move the hay off the fields, and therefore must buy automatic bale-stackers, and so on, in order to remain in business. Professional agronomists have stated that one of the most serious problems facing agriculture today is the lack of labour. It seems to me that this situation forces farmers to become involved in increased capitalization in respect of machinery, and the result is that farm improvement loans in an amount of $25,000 are inadequate today. Inflation plays a large part in this situation.
I am happy to see included in this bill a new provision that would allow farmers to use farm improvement loans to finance major repairs and overhaul of equipment. We have seen reported in the Globe and Mail-and many farmers have told me the same thing-that there are not- tractors and equipment available for purchase if the farmers wish to purchase them. In the past number of years many farmers were unable to afford the price of new equipment. This year, however, because of the higher prices for grain we find that some of them are now in a position to buy new equipment.
I have had reports from the west that equipment which had been ordered last fall still has not been delivered. What is the result? The old equipment used by the farmers will have to be repaired. I think it is time a provision was included in this legislation that would make it possible to
April 10, 1974

use the Farm Improvement Loans Act for financing repairs until such time as these farmers are in the position to obtain new equipment.
Even though this provision is included in the bill, I think we should look at the debate of April 2, 1974, when the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Nesdoly) brought forward a private member's motion which stated that many of the farmers of western Canada or of eastern Canada are not able to obtain repair parts for their equipment. We have seen examples of $12,000 or $14,000 combines and tractors sitting idle when they are required for the planting or the harvesting of crops. In the article which appeared recently in the Globe and Mail I noted that a good deal of the equipment necessary this year has been made from spare parts, and that in fact even in the United States there are increasing numbers of auction sales where new equipment is being sold at three or four times the list price. Because the farmers need it so badly, they are prepared to pay this amount in anticipation of higher prices for their agricultural products in coming years.
I think this is a serious matter, one which the Minister of Agriculture should look into. I know that he has spoken to them about it down there, but I think we should do everything in our power to see that parts are available for equipment this year and that new tractors and other new equipment will be available to meet demands in the future.
I see in the bill a clause which allows the purchase of livestock or beef stock. I assume that it also allows beef farmers to purchase equipment and make major repairs. I know that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) will be happy with this clause. A large amount of the honey produced in Canada comes from his constituency, and perhaps farmers in that area will be able to purchase some equipment to keep the bears away, because that is their major problem at present.
In clause 2 we see an amendment to increase farm improvement loans from $25,000 to $50,000. The reasons for it have been stated. Inflation is the main problem. A number of applications had to be turned down because there were simply not enough funds available for farmers to make the necessary additions to their farming operations. Farming is one of the major industries in Canada which must depend upon lending institutions and upon credit to keep the operation going from year to year. We have no major worries regarding the increase from $25,000 to $50,000 and we hope the clause will be passed as quickly as possible.
The other clauses simply add time to the bill, from July 1, 1974, to June 30, 1977, and allow institutions to lend more money than they are presently able to do. I have only one more comment to add to my brief speech on farm improvement loans. It concerns interest rates. It has been my experience that many bankers are not willing, or not as willing as they should be, to lend money to farmers under the Farm Improvement Loans Act interest rates which, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said, averaged 8.4 per cent. I think the major reason for this is consumer credit which is in such demand today with the large number of Chargex and Master Charge cards. This
Loans Acts Amendments
type of credit carries an interest rate of 12 per cent or more. Surely any wise manager of a financial institution will look more favourably on loans if he can receive 12 per cent or 14 per cent interest than he will on loans that are guaranteed but are at an average rate of 8V4 per cent.
I hope that we can ask some more questions in the committee and that the bill will be passed. I also hope the minister will consider some of the suggestions that have been made regarding certain aspects of the Farm Improvement Loans Act.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very unusual bill in which we put farmers, fishermen and small businessmen in the same package. I would suggest that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) has been remiss in his responsibility, because he should also have thrown in veterans so that the amount of loans could be doubled for them as well. This suggestion has been made in committee and would apply to the small holdings of veterans. That is what we have been asking about, and that is what the whole ball game is about.
This government does not seem able to do anything about the rising cost of commodities and inputs, the various factors that go into making up the requirements of these three sectors of our economy. The solution, therefore, is to raise the amount of money that can be borrowed by them. I think it is a sad commentary on our society that the best we can do is to say to the banks that these are not viable industries which can operate by themselves. Borrowing is not easy, therefore the banks will have to be assured of guaranteed loans or the money will not be made available for these purposes.
Since the Veterans Land Act holdings fall into the same category, I am surprised that the Minister of Veterans Affairs, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) and the minister responsible for small businesses did not get together so that the four of them could bring in this piece of legislation, rather than only three. I would like to tell the Minister of Veterans Affairs that I think this provision including veterans would have been passed as easily as will the present one which concerns the other three groups, and we would have accomplished something that everybody feels is necessary.
I say that this is a very bad way in which to do business, for a number of reasons. The first is the fact that in these three vital areas the individual who is operating at the bottom of the line in the industry is in all cases in financial difficulty and has trouble raising sufficient capital for his needs. It is a fact-my colleague the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) pointed this out-that this can be highlighted in almost any field of agriculture where production costs have gone up so rapidly that there is no comparison between the input a year ago and the input now. He used the example of binder twine. I have discussed this with a number of farmers in my area. The day of coiling hay, using a hay-hook and putting hay loose into a barn or stack has almost totally disappeared from the Canadian scene. So it is vitally necessary for us to have binder twine, and if we cannot have it we must have a substitute in the form of plastic cord of one type or another.

April 10, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
I discussed this matter with a farmer the other night over the telephone. He told me that last year he bought binder twine through the farmers' union at $5.35 a bale. This year, the co-operative with which he is dealing told him it had no twine available. I am informed that binder twine will be available, but the price will not be $5.35 or, with the 10 per cent increase, $6.50. It will be between $22 and $30 a bale. The minister shakes his head. I hope that he can give some arguments to prove that this is not so. This is an input cost to a small farmer with 30 head of cattle which is very high. It is the difference between $225 and $650, a sizeable increase in his cost of production. I understand that you can do 500 bales of hay with one bale of twine. The farmer would normally use 30 to 35 bales. The minister can do the arithmetic. I am told that farmers today will be lucky to get away this year with paying $700.
I could give examples in almost every other area, such as the cow calf operation and the cost of raising calves. We could talk about land or about fertilizer. The previous speaker mentioned machinery parts. It is not only a question of parts but a question of whether parts are available at all. Last fall I intervened on behalf of a farmer who had a David Brown tractor which had been tied up for three or four months while waiting for a very small part-incidentally, a part that was a failure in every David Brown tractor of that type. There were no parts to be had. But after I raised the roof, a part was found in transit and sent to this farmer, allowing him to get his tractor back into service. The part cost much less than $100 but the actual cost to the farmer was considerably more. This farmer's large tractor had broken down at a time when he had to do the plowing. As a result, he had to use a considerably smaller tractor and therefore his costs were two or three times greater.
I am not blaming the minister for such situations. I have great personal affection for him. We both have sat on the same committees, including the farm machinery committee. At times we both have been rebels. He knows that decisions made by that committee were made by a predecessor to it and in fact dated back ten years. But those decisions have not yet been implemented. I am still waiting for the present minister to put them into effect.
Then there is the unnatural increase in the price of the commodities that a farmer must buy. In fact, a farmer gets a hosing when he sells and also when he buys. Farmers in my area have been selling their products through Community Sales, and I suppose eventually to the packers. Members of the public are paying $3 billion in subsidy to make sure the farmer gets a fair return, but I think it is almost impossible for the individual farmer in my area to get this 7'A cents and it is almost as difficult for him to get his 5 cents using the Community Sales method.
Who is making the profit? Canada Packers are ripping off great big gobs of it. As I say, I do not blame the minister. I am sure he is aware that Canada Packers are ripping us off and that all the other packers are doing the same. There really is not much that he can do until some of his colleagues decide to intervene in the middle, in the market place, and take away the unconscionable profit that part of the industry is making. I do not believe Canada Packers when they say they were losing money

before and now they have to make up for the loss. If you look at their financial statement you see that they do not have to make up much. Their profits went up immensely over the last year or so.
The same applies to fertilizer. There really will not be any more fertilizer used this year than last year, yet the farmer has to pay considerably more money for it, that is, if he is going to get fertilizer, and in most cases he is not yet sure whether he will receive the amount of fertilizer that is necessary for the crop that he anticipates planting. In fact, the pattern of the western farmer may be repeated. For years the price of seed and of working the land, and all the other cost factors going into production, were so high and the price of the end product so low that the western farmer found there was no point in putting fertilizer on his land, and as a result did not reach maximum production.
I agree with the minister that all members of parliament, whether they represent consuming areas or producing areas, must be careful to ensure that agriculture gets the maximum return possible and that the commodity involved reaches the consumer with as little rip-off as possible. I am not suggesting that we get rid of all the in-between people. That is not possible. We operate in a modern society, using modern methods. There will always be middlemen and they will always have to make a reasonable profit. The emphasis is on "reasonable". Canada Packers and others involved must be allowed a reasonable profit. But when you look at Kraft, Mr. Speaker, their profit is not fair. It is unconscionable. They should be tarred and feathered for the profit they are making. They have developed a monopoly. One of my colleagues says we could boil them in caramel. Certainly we could boil them in Cheese Whiz if we wanted, or in any of the oil products left in the residues from Procter and Gamble and other such companies.

speechtext: We are cheesed off.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
And so is the consumer. Apparently our solution now is to guarantee the banks the right to lend farmers more money. I think a farmer borrowing more money may have to do the same thing as George Weston does. George Weston became interested in a small icecream plant in my area. In fact, I was approached in connection with a DREE grant and I was quite prepared to help get a DREE grant to expand the operation. But then the George Weston people asked a very simple question: How much profit does the plant make? When it was pointed out that it made only 4 per cent, the George Weston people said they were not interested and as far as they were concerned the government could go ahead and put whatever capital it wished into the enterprise. In fact, they said they were not interested in any industry which operated at less than 8 per cent profit.
As a result, that particular enterprise was sold to a small dairy in Timmins and is now run by a totally different group of people. The point I am making is that the farmer is not making 8 per cent on his operation or else he would not need to borrow this kind of money. If my brother were able to make 8 per cent on his business, which I suppose is capitalized at a couple of hundred thousand dollars, he
April 10, 1974

would have been paying a considerable amount in income tax over the last few years. But he has not, and neither have other farmers. They have found they have to put their money into their business and in fact have to borrow more and put that into their business too. The same applies to small businessmen.
I talked to a small businessman the other day. We discussed Kraft. He showed me the long sheets, page after page of print-out from a computer, sent to grocery stores from headquarters in Toronto. Some five or six of the pages were taken up with Kraft products that were going up in price. He has to remark and re-price the products which he gets that are on those price lists. The prices change almost week by week. I looked at three weeks of these printed sheets, particularly with respect to Kraft products, and in several instances the same product had increased in price in each of those three weeks.
The small businessman must also be in trouble. Most small grocery stores used to operate on the basis that if they kept ordering from National Grocers or Loeb's, they had a mark-up of 5 per cent or 6 per cent on canned goods, so much on meat and so much on fruit and vegetables. It was consistent and they marked up the product according to the invoice they received. That is no longer possible, because every commodity has a different mark-up which the manufacturer suggests. I am sure that is true in other fields as well. There are several plywood plants in my area, and the price of glue has increased so rapidly that one owner tells me that if the increase continues there is no point in staying in business. Every time an item used in the manufacture of plywood was re-priced, he had to re-work all his bids to customers and it was not worth the trouble. This kind of problem is arising all the time.
I am sure the cost-price squeeze is hitting fishermen too. It is a major factor in agriculture. I think it would be safe to say that most small businessmen in this country have been very independent in thought and in politics. In many cases they were selling their own personality and their own method of operation. This is true, to some extent, of the farmer as well who has been able to prosper by putting in a very long day and being very careful in his operation. He is no longer in that position, Mr. Speaker. He can no longer make decisions from week to week that will be to his advantage.
To take binder twine as an example, again, it cost $225 last year and this year it will run something over $700. How is he to recoup or take that into consideration? Does he ask for more money from the marketing board? We have gone from reasonably priced dairy rations at about 32 per cent protein to 16 per cent protein, and we are using urea as the main base of concentrates because it gives increased production. The farmer has changed his operation as far as he can, but there are many things over which he has no control. A farmer would be foolish to borrow $25,000 or $50,000 in order to expand his operation in the hope that he could solve some of his problems. Indeed, it is unlikely that his farm will produce enough to repay the interest, let alone the principal. He is likely to be involved with a large loan and yet his enterprise will show an unreasonably small profit.
Message from the Senate
Some farmers in my area are selling their farms for as much as $450,000, but I wonder about the person going into a dairy operation at that price and then borrowing another $50,000 for improvements. It is unlikely he can make a go of it because the margin is not high enough. He will have to put in some magic figure and find a way of overcoming rising costs in face of a relatively fixed income.
I suppose all hon. members will support this legislation, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, we have to support it. I strongly urge the minister to consider some of the problems that have been raised in this debate. There may be a better way to help the farmer than lending him money. I know the minister is a farmer himself and has gone to the bank upon occasion to discuss his business with the bank manager. Often the bank manager tells farmers that they are foolish to borrow more money when they cannot see their way clear to repay it. I congratulate the minister on knowing what the problems are and for taking the right tack. All we have to do now is wait and see if he can accomplish his objective. We must encourage farmers to stay in farming; we must make it possible for them to stay and to expand Canadian agriculture to the limit.
Some economists in the United States are saying that food will be so short there this summer that there will be riots. I do not know whether that is true, but I am sure there will be a great shortage of foodstuffs in the world this summer and that a large percentage of consumers in Canada will be affected. They will not have the money to buy the food they want. It is time that we took a stand with the food chains. If we are seriously aiming at being self-sufficient in foods, we must make a concerted effort in all areas. Perhaps most people do not realize it but even in sugar, which was mentioned this afternoon, we could easily be self-sufficient. At the moment we produce approximately 15 per cent of the sugar we use, but if the government guaranteed the forward price to the sugar beet producers and provided assistance for the re-establishment of refining plants in this country, we could easily be self-sufficient.
I know that the minister does not get much co-operation from the food processors in this country, but now he has a glorious opportunity to step in and put some controls on the food chains. Canada can be a major producer of agricultural products if we take the right direction. This can only come about with a healthy and viable farm population, and for that we must make available more money in the form of guaranteed bank loans.
