speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-14, to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in contributing to this debate I will restrict my remarks to those parts of the bill dealing with the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Although we welcome the amendments which will increase loans ceilings under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act from $25,000 to $50,000, I doubt if they will be of real value to fishermen of the Atlantic area and some other parts of the country. Since the act was proclaimed in 1955, less than $8 million of the money provided for under the act has been lent in the Atlantic area. There are probably a good many reasons for the lack of interest in the advantages of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act shown by fishermen of the Atlantic area.
The fact that all the Atlantic provinces have seen fit to establish provincial fisheries loan boards indicates to me that the act is not working properly in the Atlantic area. I understand that fisherman on the Pacific coast, in British Columbia, have shown more interest in loans under the act than has been the case in the Atlantic area. I understand that only 27 per cent of the moneys made available

have been lent in the Atlantic area, most of the remaining funds being lent on the Pacific coast.
In the 17 years this act has been in effect, fishermen in Newfoundland have received only 1.7 per cent of the total funds made available by the government by way of guaranteed bank loans. The province has had to establish its own fisheries loan board. Established a few years ago, the board has lent about $6 million to fishermen and has processed 2,000 applications for loans. I suspect that the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act does not appeal to Atlantic fishermen because of the high interest rates charged on loans made under the act. That, at any rate, is one reason.
As my colleague from Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said earlier, it is not easy to find a way around the high interest rates being charged by banks for these loans. Surely if the Atlantic provinces can lend fishermen money at 314 per cent, as opposed to 9!4 per cent which the banks charge under the federal scheme, it should be possible for the federal government to make these loans available at lower interest rates than those being charged.
The requirements of banks for security for loans have probably prevented Atlantic coast fishermen taking advantage of the act. As you know, fishing enterprises on the east coast are smaller in scale than those on the Pacific coast. The government should consider lowering the requirements for security for loans. Why, Mr. Speaker? If a small fishing operator loses his boat or fishing gear in a storm, he has lost his security. Thus, it is impossible for him to qualify for a loan under the act.
Also, fishermen in the Atlantic area have not availed themselves of the provisions of the act partly because of the attitude of the chartered banks with regard to lending money under the act. They do not want to lend money at rates of interest lower than those they are charging their regular customers. There is evidence to show that bank managers in my riding have been reluctant to entertain loan applications from fishermen. I suspect this holds true for the rest of the country. I suppose the reason for this is that, being in the business of making money, the banks prefer to lend it at higher interest rates than those made available under this act.
For these reasons the minister should consider establishing some system under which applications submitted by fishermen can be monitored by the department. When a fisherman submits an application to a bank for a loan under the act, a copy of that application should be sent to the appropriate government department. If that bank manager or that bank has refused to grant the loan, a government official from the appropriate department should ask the manager or the bank for an explanation. All too often when fishermen apply for loans, bank managers will impose restrictions which are not required under the act, and in many cases they prevent the fishermen from qualifying for loans. It is important for the government to keep a close eye on what happens to applications submitted by fishermen so that if there is any suggestion of banks being unfair to fishermen applying for loans something can be done.
April 10, 1974

As I say, we welcome the amendment whereby the ceiling on loans will be increased. However, I am not sure it will have the desired effect in certain parts of the country. Another reason fishermen have not taken advantage of the act is that in many small settlements in remote parts of the country there are no banking facilities. It is extremely difficult for fishermen to get to the areas where the lending agencies are established. Consequently, the government should establish some kind of mobile loan service to bring this service to the people. It should do everything in its power to encourage fishermen to avail themselves of these loans and improve their operations accordingly.
A serious problem arises from the inability of fishermen to get loans from the chartered banks. Because of the attitude of some bank officials, the fishermen are being driven into the clutches of the loan sharks. In many cases they are required to pay higher interest rates than those being charged by the banks.
Another suggestion I make to the minister is that his officials undertake a massive advertising campaign to advertise the act and explain how a fisherman should go about applying for a loan. It should state all the benefits that are available. I do not suggest that will be the entire solution to the problem. As I said earlier, the matter of interest rates being charged on these loans will have a very large bearing on whether the fishermen will want to avail themselves of this program.
I hope that the increased loan ceiling will not give the minister an excuse to reduce the amount of the federal subsidy on boat building. At the moment the subsidy amounts to 35 per cent of the actual cost of the boat. I understand that rate has not been set for the current fiscal year. I hope the minister will not attempt to reduce the amount of the subsidy by virtue of the fact he has increased the ceiling of the loans available.
I am sure there will be much more debate on this bill when it goes to committee. I look forward to questioning the minister on certain aspects of the amendments at that time. I am sure my colleagues will do likewise with regard to other aspects, namely, farm improvement loans and small businesses loans. I repeat, we welcome the amendments but are disappointed that provision is not made whereby the interest charged on the loans will be reduced.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-14, to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Colleagues of mine have spoken on the part that relates to farm improvement loans, and the hon. member who preceded me spoke about the part that relates to fisheries. I will dwell mostly on the section that relates to small businesses. This is a very important area of our economy, particularly in southwestern Ontario which is heavily populated with small businesses.
It is very important that special consideration be given to these amendments. I wish to inject a couple of ideas that will possibly improve the bill. The improvements listed in the bill are to make new businesses eligible for loans. They include loans made for the purchase of land
Loans Acts Amendments
necessary for the operation of a business as well as raising the limit from $25,000 to $50,000. Those are briefly mentioned in the recommendation. They are covered in more detail in the bill. These are fine and are very credible.
The key to small business and the progress of small businesses existing at the present time, as well as encouraging individuals with nerve and enthusiasm to launch into a new business venture, is working capital. Until now, only those who have gone through the small business exercise appreciate the lack of working capital. I have been through the small business exercise. Therefore, any comments or suggestions that I make are without any conflict of interest. I hope that at the present time my business is beyond what the act encompasses. Consequently, I am speaking without any conflict of interest.
I encourage the minister to increase the area of available working capital. I am not talking about the money referred to in the amendment which is to be used for buildings, machinery, and so on; I am talking about money to keep a business alive when receivables reach their limit of money available, as well as inventory. These two areas are the stifling points of small business. The bill refers to a limit of $1 million or less. I am thinking about businesses in the $100,000 to $200,000 bracket, or those starting from scratch.
I started my business in 1955 with practically no capital. When I think back, I must have been more mental than when I considered running as a member of parliament. However, at the moment it appears I made a success of my business. Time will tell how much success I have had as a member of parliament. When I started business I had only a few hundred dollars. When starting a new business you are brainwashed by those who sell you the material you require. They tell you, when you buy a load of equipment or feed, that you should receive the money for it before you need to buy another load. It does not work that way in the farm supply business. A farmer buys feed, fertilizer or equipment and in some cases he may have to wait for a large loan to come through from the Farm Credit Corporation, or wherever.
The small businessman is in the same category. He sells to farmers and to the agricultural trade, and in some cases farmers have to wait 2, 3 or even 6 months before their credit is approved, in some cases rightly so. Certainly loans from the Industrial Development Bank take a long time. Sometimes when they go to a bank to borrow money, even if they are willing, so to speak, to even put up their wives they have to prove they do not need the money before they actually get it. The smaller the business, the more this applies. I have gone through this, Mr. Speaker. They give it to you with one hand, and then ask you how much you can pay back with the other.
I have changed my bank several times. I remember one occasion in the late 1950s when one bank told me I could not have any more overdrafts because money was tight. I went to see another bank and put my cards on the table. I had been told by the first bank it just did not have enough money to lend, so having by now been approved by the new bank, I told the original bank I would have to move my affairs to a bigger bank. This is the kind of situation

April 10, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
small businesses are faced with. As I say, you have to prove you do not need the money before you can get it. I think the provisions of the act should be widened to permit more government risk capital. The act simply guarantees that if a loan goes sour, the government will back up the bank. A lot of individuals in this country have the idea that farm improvement and small business loans are government money. That is not so; this is bank money.
In his presentation this afternoon the minister claimed lending was at a high level. I believe this is true of farm improvement loans, but around the London area the banks have made no small business loans to speak of. The reason is that banks can lend their money at far less risk in other ways, and as a result they really do not care whether small businessmen receive loans or not. As suggested by one of my colleagues in the previous debate, one way of alleviating the situation is to oblige banks to lend this kind of money. Naturally, a ceiling would have to be placed on the extent of the loans and the banks would be obligated to reach that ceiling. Unless such a system is implemented, I can see no way to encourage the banks to make loans to small businessmen.
Perhaps it will be necessary to strengthen the government's guarantee to the banks. After all, the government is handing out money under LIP, OFY, or you name it, all of them credible in their own right. But the small businessmen of this country can become big businessmen. Let us not forget that all big businesses were at one time small. This is the sort of thing that has made Canada. During the first 100 years of confederation many small businesses grew. A man has a dream, thinks he can make something go, and armed mostly with enthusiasm, plus a lot of hard work, he builds up a business. Today there are many large businesses which 50 to 75 years ago were launched with a few hundred dollars. I have a feed business franchise that is in this category. Eighty years ago the founder of the business mixed his first bag of feed with a scoop shovel. Today the business is one of the top ten in North America. But, as I say, once it was a very small family business.
The point I am trying to make is that the government can afford to put up more risk capital to support small business. After all, even if a business goes under someone else may pick up the idea and carry it on. The banks should be made more aware of their obligations to the country and to the small business community. As I have said, I am sure some sort of a quota system for Banks to lend this risk money could be worked out. Take the case of the small business with $100,000 in receivables-which today is not a large amount-another $100,000 or better in inventory, and something happens to the economy which slows up revenue. Two or three years ago, for example, a lot of businesses literally went bankrupt as a result of a Post Office strike. These were businesses that depended on money coming in through the mails. The clients of these businesses no doubt in some cases took advantage of the situation. After all, who could prove that the cheques were not held up in the mail? Believe me, Mr. Speaker, I have gone all through this. I know all the answers and what to look for so far as trying to survive in business is concerned.
Our obligation as members of parliament is to encourage small business. I have lived this life of trying to survive in

small business, Mr. Speaker, so I think I know what it is all about. Small business cannot be successful without a lot of thought, research and planning. However, rather than some of the band-aid approaches we have seen from this government, they should take some positive action that will show further results in the next 100 years. When the bill goes to committee I shall want to discuss some of the amendments and, hopefully, put forth some of the ideas I have espoused this afternoon.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Like previous speakers, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see this bill now before the House as it is long overdue. Certainly it will help small business considerably as they go along their way. Small businesses play a very important role in the Canadian economy. They create over 50 per cent of Canada's gross national product and they pay close to 50 per cent of taxes collected by the government, while employing more than 50 per cent of the people working in Canada.
Small businesses provide the productive outlet for the energies of a large group of enterprising, independent people who attach great value to economic independence. In industries with optimum-size production units where the sales have been small, often the most efficient form of organization is provided by small business. For many reasons, because of closeness of management to operation they can effect economies which are not possible in larger businesses. Small businesses act as specialist suppliers to large companies, suppliers of parts and sub-assembly components at much lower costs than many of the larger companies. Small businesses add greatly to the variety of products and services offered to the consumer because they can flourish in a limited or specialized market which would not be worth-while or economical in many cases for large businesses to enter. In an economy which seems to be propelling itself toward larger, multiproduct companies, small businesses can provide competition both actual and potential and provide some check on the monopoly profits and inefficiency which monopoly breeds.
I am glad to see that the gross revenue allowable portion of this bill is being raised from $500,000 to $1 million and that the amount of a loan is being raised from $25,000 to $50,000. I cannot help but think back to the first session of this twenty-ninth parliament when the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) had a notice of motion on the order paper to increase the small businesses loan limit to $75,000 and government members at that time talked out the motion. We are now in April, 1974, and we have not yet seen the 1973 report, although the minister in his opening remarks quoted from it so I assume we will be getting it in the near future.
It is interesting to look back at the 1972 report-it is the latest one we have-which indicates that in the whole of 1972 only 2,846 loans were made in Canada under this act. When one looks back to the beginning of this act in 1961, he finds that more loans were made in the first year than 11 years later, there being 2,977 loans made the first year. I find it difficult to comprehend why there are so few loans made to the small business community.
April 10, 1974

If you are involved at all with small businessmen or know something about their operations, it is interesting to listen to their stories about what happens when they go to the bank in an attempt to get a loan under the Small Businesses Loans Act. I listened to the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) tell us about the difficulties farmers in his area have in getting loans under the act. The same difficulties exist with small businessmen.
A month or so ago I sent a letter to all the small businessmen in my riding and quoted some of the facts, figures and statistics from the 1972 report. I am now beginning to get some rather interesting replies. It is interesting to note that the banks have not seen fit to change their tactics over the years, and I suggest this has a direct relationship to the small number of loans made under this act in the course of a year. Since the inception of this act the banks have not been able to grant more than 2,977 loans in any one year. They have never granted 3,000 loans in a year. Let me refer to a letter which is typical of the replies I have received from my constituents. This small businessman writes:
Thank you very much for your letter regarding loans to small businesses. I read it with great interest as just at that time I was asked to guarantee to the bank a loan for purchase of a new truck by an independent trucker who works for our company.
I phoned the bank manager who claimed that he has never heard of the Small Businesses Loans Act, and anyway he would not be interested in a loan at 8 'A per cent interest rate. After I pointed out to him that this is a federal statute, that the trucker needs $19,000 for the new truck and that he is selling his old truck for $4,000, the manager promised to check with the head office. The reply was that it is true that truckers qualify under Small Businesses Loans Act, but in this particular case the applicant is not eligible for a loan as he owes some money to his father and to another bank.
I wonder how many businesses exist where young owners do not owe any money, whether it is to purchase furniture or a car. In this particular case the bank would gladly take over the other bank's loan
